content: When considering tuberculosis preventive treatment (TPT), it is essential to evaluate factors such as age, safety, drug-drug interactions, and adherence. National programs must carefully assess their country-specific context, available resources, and the capacity of their healthcare systems. The introduction and scale-up of shorter, safer TPT regimens are expected to improve treatment coverage, adherence, and completion rates. Historically, six or nine months of daily isoniazid (6H or 9H) has been the most widely used TPT regimen globally. However, it is anticipated that isoniazid will increasingly be replaced by rifamycin-based regimens, which are becoming more affordable and feasible. These regimens are supported by growing evidence of their efficacy and safety across various populations. Despite this shift, 6H or 9H will remain an important option, particularly in settings where rifamycin-based regimens cannot be used. In such cases, a triple-pill combination of isoniazid, cotrimoxazole, and vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) may be considered for people living with HIV (PLHIV), as it is available at a discounted price through the Stop TB Partnership’s Global Drug Facility. Isoniazid is the preferred regimen for HIV-infected children on protease inhibitor-based regimens (e.g., lopinavir-ritonavir), nevirapine, or integrase inhibitors (e.g., dolutegravir) due to potential drug-drug interactions. Additionally, isoniazid monotherapy is protective for contacts of TB patients with laboratory-confirmed isoniazid-susceptible but rifampicin-resistant TB. Shorter regimens, such as three months of weekly isoniazid plus rifapentine (3HP) or one month of daily isoniazid plus rifapentine (1HP), are viable options for national programs. Both regimens have demonstrated similar efficacy to isoniazid monotherapy for TB prevention, although no direct head-to-head comparison between 1HP and 3HP has been conducted. However, due to limited data on appropriate dosing of 1HP in children under 13 years, the World Health Organization (WHO) currently recommends 1HP only for individuals aged 13 years and older. Rifampicin-based regimens, such as four months of daily rifampicin (4R), have a long history of use in TB treatment and are associated with a favorable safety profile and lower cost compared to rifapentine. This regimen is particularly useful for contacts of individuals with isoniazid-resistant but rifampicin-susceptible TB. However, concerns about preserving rifampicin for first-line TB treatment and the potential for increased rifampicin resistance in the community must be addressed. To date, there is no evidence that scaling up TPT services has significantly increased rifampicin resistance. For young children under five years of age, who are at higher risk of progressing to severe TB disease, the three-month daily isoniazid plus rifampicin regimen (3HR) is a well-tolerated and child-friendly option. Dispersible fixed-dose combination (FDC) formulations of isoniazid and rifampicin are available and widely used for TB treatment in children. These formulations should be preferred over single pills to reduce the pill burden. In the medium to long term, 3HP or 1HP may become the preferred regimens across all age groups, provided evidence on appropriate dosing, safety, and tolerability in children under two years of age is established. The shorter duration of treatment with 3HP and its higher rates of treatment completion make it a cost-effective option. In the meantime, 3HR can be used for young children. Pregnant women can safely use certain TPT regimens, such as 6H or 3HR, although caution is required due to limited safety data for some regimens during pregnancy. Vitamin K supplementation is recommended for both the mother and infant if rifampicin is used in the last weeks of pregnancy to prevent bleeding complications. Pyridoxine (vitamin B6) supplementation is recommended for individuals at risk of peripheral neuropathy, such as those with malnutrition, chronic alcohol dependence, HIV infection, renal failure, diabetes, or those who are pregnant or breastfeeding. The standard prophylactic dose of pyridoxine is 10–25 mg/day. Routine supplementation is not necessary for otherwise healthy individuals receiving standard-dose isoniazid, but its absence should not delay TPT initiation. For established isoniazid-induced peripheral neuropathy, higher therapeutic doses of pyridoxine (50–200 mg/day) may be required. National programs should progressively transition to shorter rifamycin-based regimens due to their better safety profiles and higher likelihood of treatment completion. Training healthcare workers, developing standard operating procedures, and leveraging existing TB and HIV services are critical for successful TPT implementation and scale-up.
